issues: Littré gives the sentence with no author, as its own example under sense 2 of 'privé'. So 'Maxim quoted in Littré' suggests a sourced citation that is not there.

'Commonly attributed to Royer-Collard' leaves out that Littré's own REMARQUE on the same page questions that attribution. It quotes Édouard Fournier (Feuilleton de la Patrie, 14 July 1868): 'J'ai cru d'abord, comme bien des gens. que c'était Royer-Collard [qui avait créé cette expression]… Depuis quelque temps j'ai des doutes'. It then cites a Stendhal letter of 31 Oct. 1823 that credits the phrase to Talleyrand ('comme l'a si bien dit M. de Talleyrand, doit être murée'). The speaker field should reflect the dispute.

fieldFixes.speaker: Littré, Dictionnaire de la langue française (an example given with no author; the 'wall of private life' is variously credited to Royer-Collard or Talleyrand)
fieldFixes.note: The wall as the emblem of privacy, in one line. Translation: "Private life must be walled in; it is not permitted to seek out and make known what happens in a private person's house." Littré prints the sentence with no author, as an example of 'vie privée'. In a remark on the same entry, Littré quotes Édouard Fournier (1868), who first thought Royer-Collard coined 'the wall of private life'. Fournier then doubted it because an 1823 letter by Stendhal credits Talleyrand. So credit the sentence to Littré.

issues: The note calls Semayne's Case 'The source of "a man's home is his castle"'. That overstates it. In the same resolution Coke grounds the rule in older authority: Year Book citations (3 Edw. 3; 26 Ass.; 21 Hen. 7. 39) and the maxim 'domus sua cuique est tutissimum refugium'. The passage is the classic legal statement of the idea, not its origin.

Text variant: the Liberty Fund text used here reads 'as well for defence against injury and violence'. The standard report (5 Co. Rep. 91a, 77 E.R. 194, as quoted on Wikipedia's Semayne's case page) reads 'as well for his defence against injury and violence'. The record's quote is verbatim to its cited source, but readers comparing editions will notice the difference.

The Liberty Fund page's own framing is wrong: it calls Coke 'the English judge' who 'declared in a ruling'. In 1604 Coke was Attorney General and reported the case. The King's Bench judges (Popham CJ, Gawdy, Fenner, Yelverton, Williams JJ) decided it. The record's speaker field ('reporting Semayne's Case') is correct, so do not copy the Liberty Fund framing into the prose.

fieldFixes.note: The classic legal statement of "a man's home is his castle" - privacy as a wall the law will defend. Coke, then Attorney General, reported the King's Bench resolution and grounded it in older authority ("domus sua cuique est tutissimum refugium"). Note "for his repose": rest and quiet, not only safety. Standard editions (5 Co. Rep. 91a, 77 E.R. 194) read "as well for his defence"; the Liberty Fund text omits "his".
